raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 30-year-old male had a history of multiple episodes of hypertensive anterior uveitis in his left eye (LE) since the age of 25. He had undergone cataract surgery for a bilateral congenital cataract at the age of 3 (right eye, RE) and 18 (left eye, LE), despite an unremarkable gestational/neonatal history. Those uveitis attacks responded well to topical loteprednol, with rapid normalization of the intraocular pressure (IOP). Three years later, the patient developed hypertensive anterior uveitis in his RE. Signs and symptoms were similar to those of previous episodes in the LE. However, this time the response to loteprednol was poor, requiring the use of continuous 1% prednisolone drops. As they were tapered, the intraocular inflammation relapsed. Oral valacyclovir was also attempted, with no improvement in the number or the severity of relapses in RE.
Extensive uveitis workup was negative (including rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, serology for syphilis, angiotensin converting enzyme and HLA-B27). IgG for HSV (herpes simplex virus), VZV (varicella zoster virus), CMV and rubella viruses were positive, but with negative IgM for these viruses.
At this time, the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in the RE and 20/25 in the LE. Slit-lamp examination (SLE) of the RE revealed ciliary injection, mild corneal edema and a few nummular keratic precipitates (KPs) inferiorly, in addition to iris heterochromia (Figure 1). Minimal inflammation in the anterior chamber (AC), with 0.5+ cell and 1+ flare, could also be seen in the RE. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 45 mmHg in the RE. SLE and IOP of LE were within normal limits. The fundus examination was also normal in both eyes.
As a consequence of the clinical course with multiple episodes of hypertensive anterior uveitis, associated with minimal AC inflammation and sparse nummular KPs, in addition to the lack of response to valacyclovir, the possibility of CMV etiology was considered and an AC tap was performed in the RE. PCR results were positive for CMV, but negative for HSV, VZV, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus), and also for human herpesviruses 6, 7 and 8.
The patient was then successfully treated with topical 0.15% ganciclovir gel (initially 5x/day for 2 months, followed by 2x/day) and dexamethasone drops (once daily), for a period of one year. Remission was achieved for 2 years.
However, a new recurrence with mild intraocular inflammation, elevation of IOP and corneal edema led to the restart of the antiviral. The patient restarted the treatment with ganciclovir (at this time 2% drops 5x/day, in addition to 0.15% gel at bedtime) and topical dexamethasone, with subsequent resolution of the intraocular inflammation, and no recurrences after 3 years of further follow-up, now with topical 0.15% ganciclovir gel.
The specular microscopy revealed a significantly decreased endothelial cell count (1,366 cells/mm2 in the RE, compared to 2,106 cells/mm2 in the LE).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old previously healthy male presented with recurrent episodes of unilateral hypertensive anterior uveitis in the right eye refractory to topical loteprednol and oral valacyclovir.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having undergone bilateral congenital cataract extractions at ages 3 (right eye) and 18 (left eye), the patient first experienced recurrent hypertensive anterior uveitis in the left eye at age 25 (controlled with topical loteprednol) and subsequently developed recurrent right-eye hypertensive anterior uveitis at age 28. Over a 2-year period, right-eye flares occurred twice yearly, consistently relapsed whenever topical 1% prednisolone acetate was tapered, and failed to respond to empirical oral valacyclovir.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bilateral congenital cataracts status post cataract extraction at age 3 years in the right eye and age 18 years in the left eye; unremarkable gestational and neonatal history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for systemic rheumatologic or infectious symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and 20/25 in the left eye (LE). Right-eye slit-lamp examination revealed ciliary injection, mild corneal edema, sparse inferiorly distributed medium-sized nummular keratic precipitates (KPs), iris heterochromia, mild anterior chamber reaction (0.5+ cells and 1+ flare), and markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) of 45 mmHg. Left-eye slit-lamp exam, LE IOP, and bilateral dilated fundoscopic examinations were unremarkable. Specular microscopy later showed reduced corneal endothelial cell density in the RE (1,366 cells/mm2 vs 2,106 cells/mm2 in the LE).
objective.routine_investigations: Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, syphilis serology, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), and HLA-B27 were all negative. Serum IgG was positive and IgM was negative for HSV, VZV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and rubella.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic anterior chamber aqueous humor paracentesis of the right eye with multiplex PCR was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA and negative for HSV, VZV, EBV, HHV-6, HHV-7, and HHV-8.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Right-eye cytomegalovirus (CMV) chronic hypertensive anterior uveitis (presenting with Posner-Schlossman-like intraocular hypertension, Fuchs-like iris heterochromia, and corneal endothelial cell loss) in an immunocompetent pseudophakic adult, confirmed by positive aqueous humor CMV PCR. Treatment with topical 0.15% ganciclovir gel (5 times daily for 2 months, then twice daily) and once-daily topical dexamethasone for 1 year achieved a 2-year remission; a subsequent mild hypertensive relapse resolved after restarting topical 2% ganciclovir drops (5 times daily) plus bedtime 0.15% ganciclovir gel and topical dexamethasone, and the patient remained recurrence-free for 3 years on maintenance topical 0.15% ganciclovir gel.
